How does 'To Feed Is to Suffer' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"He turns his mind away from those phenomena, and having done so, inclines his mind to the property of deathlessness: ‘This is peace, this is exquisite—the resolution of all fabrications; the relinquishment of all acquisitions; the ending of craving; dispassion; cessation; unbinding.’” — AN 9:36
Even though the Buddha uses a martial simile to explain this contemplation, many of the similes he recommends for actually inducing a state of disenchantment with concentration use feeding analogies."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.

In 'To Feed Is to Suffer', how are we advised to handle suffering (dukkha) and emotional stress?

The text teaches: *"For example:
“Just as a royal frontier fortress has large stores of tonics—ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, & salt—for the delight, convenience, & comfort of those within, and to ward off those without; in the same way the disciple of the noble ones, with the abandoning of pleasure & pain, as with the earlier disappearance of joys & distresses, enters & remains in the fourth jhāna—purity of equanimity & mindfulness, neither-pleasure-nor-pain—for his own delight, convenience, & comfort, and to alight on unbinding.” — AN 7:63
At the same time, concentration needs to be fed, both physically and mentally."* Rather than running away from discomfort or trying to suppress it, the Thai Forest approach is to turn around and investigate suffering directly (*dukkha-sacca*). Notice that suffering is not a permanent fixture of the heart; it is a conditioned experience arising from attachment and craving (*taṇhā*). When observed with still, patient awareness, the knot of tension naturally unwinds.

How does 'To Feed Is to Suffer' present the dynamics of Dependent Arising (paṭiccasamuppāda)?

The text explains: *"There we find that he depicted the interplay of conditions in dependent co-arising in another manner entirely."* Dependent Arising demonstrates how ignorance (*avijjā*) triggers mental concocting (*saṅkhāra*), leading to consciousness, sensory contact, feeling, and craving. When ignorance is replaced by direct knowing through insight (*paññā*), the entire chain of conditional suffering uncouples in reverse (*paṭiloma*), revealing the unconditioned Nibbāna.
